questions.q: What does this lesson say makes a component genuinely reusable across different callers?
options: Having as many @api properties as possible, regardless of whether a given caller needs them
Never using slots, since slots make a component harder to reuse
Deliberately designed interface: exposing exactly the knobs a caller actually needs through @api and slots, and firing events for exactly the things a caller might react to
Hardcoding the component's styling so every caller sees it exactly the same way
questions.explain: Reusability comes from deliberate interface design -- exposing exactly the right knobs through @api and slots, and firing events for exactly what a caller might want to react to, nothing more and nothing less.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a 'feature component' and a 'generic component' as defined in this lesson?
options: A feature component is built for one specific business purpose and can be tightly coupled to its data; a generic component is built for a general-shaped need and should know nothing about a specific business object
Feature components are always smaller in file size than generic components
Generic components cannot use @api properties, only slots
There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable
questions.explain: A feature component (like openCaseList) is fine being coupled to its specific business purpose. A generic component (like statusBadge or confirmModal) should work for any caller with that general shape of need, with no business-object-specific knowledge baked in.

questions.q: What is the trap this lesson warns about with a component like `statusBadge`?
options: statusBadge should never be built as a reusable component under any circumstance
Generic components are always slower to render than feature components
statusBadge components cannot accept any @api properties
A generic-sounding name can hide a component that's secretly a feature component -- for example, hardcoding Case status values makes it unusable for Opportunity stages without a rewrite
questions.explain: The trap is a component whose name sounds generic but whose implementation secretly bakes in assumptions specific to one business object -- which defeats the purpose of calling it generic in the first place.

questions.q: In the composition example, why does building one generic `dataTablePanel` plus thin feature components (like `openCaseList`) scale better than three separate, nearly identical table components?
options: Because Salesforce limits orgs to a fixed number of total components
Because feature components cannot use slots, only generic components can
Because a styling or behavior fix to the shared generic component only has to happen once, and every feature component built on top of it benefits immediately
Because generic components are automatically exposed to Lightning App Builder
questions.explain: Composition concentrates shared behavior and styling in one place. Fixing the generic dataTablePanel once automatically benefits every feature component built on top of it, instead of requiring the same fix to be repeated in multiple near-duplicate components.

questions.q: Which of these is a sign, per this lesson, that a component has taken on too many responsibilities?
options: It imports Apex methods or object-specific schema references directly, inside what's supposed to be a reusable, presentation-only component
It exposes a single, well-named @api property
It uses a default slot for its body content
It fires a custom event when the user clicks a button
questions.explain: A presentation-only, reusable component importing Apex methods or object-specific schema references directly is a sign it has absorbed business logic that should instead live in a thin feature component built on top of it.
